en: A mutation that lets a bacterium survive an antibiotic is beneficial for that microbe but harmful for a sick person, so effect depends on whose survival you mean.
Harmful mutations can change a protein's shape so a cell process fails, which secondary biology pages use as the usual disease example without naming a scare list.
A rare mutation in a human immune receptor can reduce HIV infection risk, a beneficial example sources discuss, not a reason to seek infection.
A mutation that blocks chlorophyll is harmful for a green plant because it can no longer harvest sunlight well, a plant example of a damaging change.
A color mutation may hide a moth on dark bark but expose it on pale bark, showing that beneficial versus harmful depends on the environment.
Mutations that switch a needed gene off are often harmful, which is why sources treat many knock-out changes as damaging unless the gene was unused.
A mutation that gives a new activity can be beneficial, harmful, or both, so secondary sources refuse a single label without naming the trait.
RNA viruses mutate quickly; some changes help the virus spread and are harmful to hosts, an example of benefit and harm at two levels.
Some fruit mutations that stop seeds can be useful to farmers and eaters even if they would be harmful for the plant in the wild.
If one website calls every mutation dangerous, check a textbook: the three-way split into help, harm, and no effect is the consensus view.
Ultraviolet light can damage DNA and raise mutation rate; whether each change helps, hurts, or does nothing is a separate later question.
Cells proofread DNA copies, so many mistakes never become mutations; sources mention this when they explain why not every copying error is harmful.
A harmful mutation can hide if one good copy of the gene still works, so sources warn that 'no effect now' is not always 'never harmful'.
Much DNA does not code for protein; many letter changes there are scored neutral unless a control switch was hit, a distinction textbooks make.
Whole-genome duplications in plants can be beneficial by making bigger fruits or new species, a large mutation sources treat as sometimes helpful.
Class facts may name disease as a harmful effect, but they should not tell anyone they are ill; that judgment belongs to a clinician and a sourced test.
Neutral does not mean 'nothing happened in the DNA'; it means the change did not clearly help or hurt the organism's function or survival.
Human-gene databases list many harmful variants, so they can bias a report unless you also sample sources that discuss neutral and beneficial cases.
Plant breeders sometimes keep beneficial mutations for yield or disease resistance, then write those examples in agricultural science sources.
Some inherited color-vision changes are treated as harmful for certain tasks and nearly neutral for others, a reminder to name the job when labeling an effect.
Changes in already-broken genes are often scored neutral because those sequences were not making a needed protein anyway.
Beneficial means better survival or reproduction in a stated setting, not 'good' in a moral sense, a wording secondary biology sources keep careful.
Oxygen sits in group 16 of the periodic table, so it has six valence electrons, the ones in its outer shell.
To find oxygen's valence electrons, find oxygen on the table and read its main-group number: group 16 means six outer electrons.
On older tables oxygen is in group VIA; the Roman six is the same count: oxygen has six valence electrons.
For groups 13 to 18, subtract ten from the group number: oxygen is group 16, and 16 minus 10 is six valence electrons.
Oxygen is in period 2, so its valence shell is the second shell, which holds those six outer electrons.
Oxygen's atomic number is eight: two electrons fill the inner shell, leaving six as valence electrons in the outer shell.
A simple shell pattern for oxygen is two, then six; the six is the valence count you also get from its column on the table.
Six valence electrons means oxygen is two short of a full set of eight, which is why it often forms two bonds.
